catalog_quote: Bawman 1949 pp. 42-43: «II. Do acento: (1). Acentuação das sílabas. O acento tónico em Lomue, parece dever colocar-se o mais atrás possível, e nisto difere o Lomue do Yao e Nyanja em que as palavras se acentuam de preferência na penúltima sílaba. O acento em Lomue é muitas vezes colocado na antepenúltima ou mesmo antes. À parte um pequeno número de casos o acento não recai sobre a última sílaba. Nesses poucos casos, cono [sic] no possessivo da 2.ª pessoa do singular, é isso provàvelmente devido à perda de uma sílaba final breve. Exemplo: empa yawá, sua casa (de você) igual a: empa yawao.» Part 2, p. 209: «Káhirwa, Se eu não vier. Nota: O acento está sobre a primeira sílaba.»; p. 213: «Wárwaka, rwaka ni mwará. Quando vieres, trás a tua mulher. ... Nota: O acento é aqui transportado para a primeira sílaba.» || Kisseberth 2003 pp. 553-554: “There is no variety of Makhuwa known to us where there is anything resembling a fully articulated system of lexical tone contrasts. Verb stems exhibit no lexical contrasts whatsoever. High tone is assigned to a particular mora or moras in the stem on the basis of the morphology in which the stem is inserted. Assignment of H tone may be to the first, second, third, or last stem mora, and in some cases to both the first and the third. ... In the more ‘central’ varieties of Makhuwa (inland Nampula province) and in Lomwe varieties, primary High tones simply surface wherever they occur, without further ado.”
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: There is no variety of Makhuwa known to us where there is anything resembling a fully articulated system of lexical tone contrasts. Verb stems exhibit no lexical contrasts whatsoever. High tone is assigned to a particular mora or moras in the stem on the basis of the morphology in which the stem is inserted. [...] High tones that are assigned to moras on the basis of either lexical or morphological considerations will be referred to as primary H tones [...]. In the more 'central' varieties of Makhuwa (inland Nampula province) and in Lomwe varieties, primary High tones simply surface wherever they occur, without further ado. However, in many other dialects there is a systematic phenomenon of tone doubling.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lomwe (as part of the Makhuwa cluster) is described as a restricted/predictable tone language: High tones are placed on stem moras by morphology (verbs) or noun class (nominals), with a marginal lexical penult-vs-final H contrast in bimoraic class 7/9 noun stems in Lomwe; Lomwe lacks tone doubling. The source gives no statement about word stress or accent placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical H-placement contrast in bimoraic cl. 7(9)/8(10) noun stems 'in some central dialects (as well as in Lomwe)' (e-hopá 'fish' vs e-nári 'buffalo', p. 553); loanword exceptions to class-based H placement (ni-gurudúumu 'wheel').
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described for words in IP-final vs IP-medial position (tone doubling blocked phrase-finally in doubling dialects; Lomwe has no doubling). Statement is made for the Makhuwa dialect cluster with explicit mention of Lomwe varieties; author's Lomwe data from Mucuba district, Zambezia.
new_statements.identity_note: Kisseberth 2003 treats Lomwe as part of the Makhuwa (P30) dialect continuum and states his tone generalisations for 'Makhuwa' with explicit remarks on 'Lomwe varieties'; his own Lomwe observations are from Mucuba district, Zambezia (i.e. Mozambique Lomwe, lomw1241). Other opened sources concern the same cluster: Visser 2015 describes Lomwe-Mihavani of Malawi (Glottolog Malawi Lomwe, mala1256); Ngunga & Faquir 2011 list Elomwe as a variant of Emakhuwa (vmw, makh1264). No opened source gives a stress rule for any Lomwe variety.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. 2003. Makhuwa (P30). In Derek Nurse & Gerard Philippson (eds.), The Bantu Languages, 546-568. London: Routledge.
sources.quote: There is no variety of Makhuwa known to us where there is anything resembling a fully articulated system of lexical tone contrasts. Verb stems exhibit no lexical contrasts whatsoever. High tone is assigned to a particular mora or moras in the stem on the basis of the morphology in which the stem is inserted. [...] High tones that are assigned to moras on the basis of either lexical or morphological considerations will be referred to as primary H tones [...]. In the more 'central' varieties of Makhuwa (inland Nampula province) and in Lomwe varieties, primary High tones simply surface wherever they occur, without further ado. However, in many other dialects there is a systematic phenomenon of tone doubling.
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Sec. 3.4 'Tone' (pp. 553-555): no fully articulated lexical tone contrasts in any Makhuwa variety; H assigned morphologically to stem moras; nominal H location predictable from noun class, except a penult-vs-final H contrast in bimoraic cl.7/9 stems 'in some central dialects (as well as in Lomwe)'; 'in Lomwe varieties, primary High tones simply surface wherever they occur' (no tone doubling).
